A_target.statement:
Let $S$ be a [[Definition:Set|set]].
Then there is no [[Definition:Surjection|surjection]]:
:$f: S \to \powerset S$

B_source.statement:
Let $\sequence {r_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be a family of [[Definition:Mapping|mappings]] $r_i: I \to X$, where $X$ has at least two elements.
Then there exists $d: I \to X$ such that:
:$\forall i \in I: \map d i \ne \map {r_i} i$
In particular $d \ne r_i$ for every $i$.

substitutions.the constructed anti-diagonal object: D = {i in S : i not in f(i)}

derived.no row equals d: no element maps to D, so f is not onto

validity_conditions: For any i, D and f(i) disagree on membership of i (by construction of D), so D != f(i).
Hence D in P(S) is not in the image of f, so f is not surjective.
The construction is the diagonal argument instantiated with 'row i = f(i)' and 'flip the diagonal'.
proof_plan:
Let $f: S \to \powerset S$ be any [[Definition:Mapping|mapping]].
Define:
:$D = \set {i \in S: i \notin \map f i}$

For each $i \in S$:
:$i \in D \iff i \notin \map f i$
Hence $D \ne \map f i$.
Thus $D$ is not in the [[Definition:Image of Mapping|image]] of $f$.

As $f$ was arbitrary, no $f: S \to \powerset S$ is a [[Definition:Surjection|surjection]].
{{qed}}
